chunks.text: Japan has an overall safety risk rated as very-low. Violent crime is very-low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is low. The US State Department advises: Exercise Normal Precautions. Exercise normal precautions in Japan. U.S. citizens should always exercise caution when traveling abroad. For solo female travelers: Very safe. Some train cars have women-only sections during rush hour. Groping (chikan) on crowded trains is a known issue — women-only cars are the safest option.. LGBTQ+ safety: Generally safe but limited legal protections. Same-sex marriage not recognized. PDA is uncommon for all couples. Discrimination is rare but LGBTQ+ visibility is limited outside Tokyo's Shinjuku Ni-chome.. Natural disaster risks include: earthquakes, typhoons, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions.

In Japan, call 110 for police, 119 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 119 for fire services. Police and fire/ambulance use different numbers. English support is limited — ask hotel staff for help if possible. The U.S. Embassy Tokyo in Tokyo can be reached at +81-3-3224-5000.

Japan has a Universal (National Health Insurance) healthcare system, rated excellent quality. Typical costs for tourists: Tourists pay full price without insurance. A basic clinic visit costs $50-150. Emergency room visits $200-800. Hospital stays $300-1,000/night. Dental visits $50-200.. Pharmacy access: Pharmacies (yakkyoku) are widespread. Many OTC medications available including pain relievers and cold medicine. Prescription drugs require a local prescription — foreign prescriptions are not accepted.. Hospital quality is excellent. Most staff speak limited English — major hospitals in Tokyo, Osaka, and Kyoto have international departments with English-speaking staff. St. Luke's International Hospital (Tokyo) and AMDA International Medical Information Center can help locate English-speaking doctors. Recommended vaccinations: Routine, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Japanese Encephalitis (if rural/extended stay). Malaria risk is negligible. Travel insurance advice: Travel insurance strongly recommended. Japanese hospitals typically require upfront payment in cash or credit card — insurance reimbursement happens after. Medevac coverage recommended for remote areas.

Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Japan. Strictly prohibited under the Stimulants Control Act. Carrying even with a valid foreign prescription can result in arrest and imprisonment. There is no exemption process.
Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) is banned in Japan. Prohibited as it contains stimulant precursors. Use alternative decongestants like phenylephrine.
Codeine is restricted in Japan. Allowed in small quantities (up to 1 month supply) with a Yakkan Shoumei import certificate and doctor's letter.
CBD / cannabis products is banned in Japan. All cannabis-derived products are illegal regardless of THC content. CBD oil, edibles, and topicals are prohibited.
Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta) is restricted in Japan. Allowed with a Yakkan Shoumei import certificate. Must carry original prescription and doctor's letter. Maximum 1 month supply.
Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Japan. Some benzodiazepines are controlled. Allowed with Yakkan Shoumei for up to 1 month supply with documentation.

Travel advisory for Japan: overall risk level is low. Normal precautions apply for Japan. US State Department: Exercise normal precautionin Japan.
U.S. citizens should always exercise caution when traveling abroad. Use these general tips to stay safe.

Scam alert in Fukuoka, Japan — The Nakasu Girls Bar ¥1,000,000 Overcharge (nightlife, severity: high). Street hustlers lure visitors into girls bars in Nakasu where hostesses continuously serve drinks without quoting prices. Bills escalate dramatically—documented cases range from ¥400,000 to over ¥1,000,000 for three hours. Bouncers block exits when customers question charges. Some venues have yakuza affiliations. How to avoid: Never follow street hustlers into Nakasu venues. Patronize only Google Maps-listed establishments with 4.5+ stars and 50+ English reviews. Demand printed menus with prices before ordering. Leave immediately if seated without pricing information. Call 110 if pressured, citing Fukuoka's Bottakuri Prevention Ordinance.

Scam alert in Fukuoka, Japan — The Nakasu Yatai Foreign-Tourist Overcharge (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Riverside yatai food stalls systematically overcharge foreign tourists while charging local prices to Japanese customers. A ¥3,200 order becomes ¥5,600. Reviews confirm this targeting pattern is widespread and deliberate, with locals avoiding these tourist-facing stalls. How to avoid: Eat at Tenjin yatai instead, particularly Nagahama. Photograph menus before sitting. Refuse stalls where hustlers recruited you from the street. Demand itemized receipts before paying. Prioritize stalls with 4.5+ star ratings from Japanese reviewers.

Scam alert in Fukuoka, Japan — The Hakata Station Tsukushi-guchi Hustler Shakedown (nightlife, severity: high). Organized hustler groups operate at Hakata Station's east exit, approaching visitors with low-price drink offers (quoted as ¥3,000) that balloon to ¥15,000–30,000. Hustlers earn 10–20% commission per customer. Inside venues, unrequested appetizers and service charges are added. Top earners pull ¥500,000 monthly. How to avoid: Use Hakata-guchi (west) exit instead. Ignore all hustlers—avoid eye contact and engagement. Select restaurants on Google Maps or Tabelog before arriving. Call 110 if pressured. Note that Fukuoka posted anti-kyakuhiki warning signs at Tsukushi-guchi since 2020.

Scam alert in Fukuoka, Japan — The Tinder / Matching App Bar Lure (nightlife, severity: high). Users matching on Tinder or Bumble with women who suggest meeting at specific Nakasu or Tenjin bars encounter massive bills (¥40,000–80,000 for minimal drinks and food). The woman is paid per delivered customer and typically vanishes before the bill arrives. Named venues include PIGLET bar on the 3rd floor of Yamamoto Building near Nakasukawabata Station. How to avoid: Insist on venues you select from Google Maps with visible street presence and 4.5+ reviews. Unmatch if she refuses your suggestion. Suggest daytime coffee or walks before drinks. Leave if warning signs appear (upper floor, no signage, she knows staff). Screenshot named problematic venues to pattern-match.

Scam alert in Fukuoka, Japan — The Booking.com 'Cash in the Fridge' Rental Scam (money, severity: high). You book an apartment near Hakata Station on Booking.com for around ¥18,000 a night and pay in full. The night before check-in, the host messages you on LINE — not through Booking.com — with an apology: '¥50,500 cleaning deposit wasn't added to the listing; please leave it in an envelope inside the refrigerator when you arrive, or the door code won't work.' The property is a converted 1LDK in a multi-tenant building with no name on the intercom. The deposit is never refunded, Booking.com has no chat record because everything moved to LINE, and the operator is usually running an unlicensed Minpaku in violation of Japan's Private Lodging Business Act. How to avoid: Keep every message inside the Booking.com or Airbnb chat. Any host who moves the conversation to LINE, WhatsApp, or email and then asks for extra cash is running a scam — report the listing through the platform's 'report listing' flow and refuse to pay. Booking.com and Airbnb will refund you if you never paid the cash and will investigate if you did. For stays of three nights or more in Fukuoka, prefer hotels over Minpaku: Hotel Forza Hakata-guchi and Richmond Hotel Hakata Ekimae are both under ¥15,000 a night and fully licensed.

Scam alert in Fukuoka, Japan — The Hakata Station Phishing Approach (transport, severity: moderate). You've just stepped off the Shinkansen at Hakata Station with a roller bag in each hand. A friendly man in a lanyard steps up: 'Tourism survey — can I photograph your passport for the visitor count?' The lanyard is homemade, the badge is a laminated print, and the 'survey' is a data harvest. Within 48 hours, either someone calls your hotel impersonating you and talks the front desk into your folio, or unfamiliar charges appear on the card you linked to your passport at check-in. A common variant waits at the taxi stand: a man in a suit quotes ¥8,000 flat to your hotel instead of the metered ¥1,500 fare, and once you're belted in, he extends the route through Kego. How to avoid: Never hand your passport to anyone who isn't in uniform behind a desk. If someone asks for passport details or your hotel name on the platform or in the taxi rank, say 'sumimasen' and walk to the nearest uniformed station attendant — one is posted at the central Chikushi-guchi exit at almost all hours. From the airport, take the Fukuoka City Subway Kuko Line (¥270, five minutes to Hakata) instead of a taxi. At the taxi rank itself, board only cars in the official queue with green license plates, and ignore anyone who approaches you directly.

Scam alert in Hiroshima, Japan — The Nagarekawa-Shintenchi Hustler Shakedown (nightlife, severity: high). Hustlers in suits approach tourists in Hiroshima's entertainment district offering nightlife venues. Once inside, establishments with no visible pricing charge exorbitant amounts—one 2023 case involved a ¥830,000 charge. A 2019 police operation disbanded a 20-person hustler network delivering 281 customers in a single night. How to avoid: Never follow hustlers anywhere in Nagarekawa, Yakkenbori, or Shintenchi. Avoid free information centers designed to steer customers to commission-paying venues. Research bars on Google Maps or Tabelog before arrival (4.3+ rating, 50+ reviews). Walk out immediately if no printed menu with prices is available. Call 110 if pressured.

Scam alert in Hiroshima, Japan — The Okonomiyaki Tourist Overcharge (money, severity: moderate). You order a single Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki at a restaurant in Shintenchi — the menu on the wall says ¥1,200. The pancake arrives, is excellent, and twenty minutes later the handwritten bill is ¥1,700. When you point at the menu, the server 'explains' that the ¥1,200 was for the basic version and you got the deluxe, or that prices went up last week and the wall hasn't been updated. A December 2024 TripAdvisor case documented a party of four billed ¥4,000 on an order that totaled ¥3,300 on the menu, with the receipt itself altered in pen. How to avoid: Photograph the wall menu with your phone before you order — a timestamped photo ends the dispute on the spot. When the bill arrives, ask for a 'meisaisho' (明細書 — itemized receipt); if staff refuse or stall, pay only the menu price and leave. Stick to named okonomiyaki houses in Okonomimura (Reichan and Hassho both sit on the 4-star line with 500+ Japanese reviews); drift into no-name shops in side streets only if the posted menu looks complete and prices are visible from the sidewalk.

Scam alert in Hiroshima, Japan — The Miyajima Deer Food-Grab Attack (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Miyajima deer, banned from commercial feeding since the 2010s, have become aggressive toward tourists carrying food or bags. Documentation includes gorings, kicks, and bites. A 4.96 million visitor count in 2025 increased confrontations, with incidents ranging from bites while eating ice cream to sustained chasing. How to avoid: Finish any food before boarding the ferry or eat only inside restaurants. Carry food in opaque backpacks or zipped bags, never plastic convenience bags. Do not feed deer or touch them for photos. If charged, drop the bag item and walk away briskly without running or pushing.

Scam alert in Hiroshima, Japan — The Miyajima Restaurant Card-Retry Triple Charge (money, severity: moderate). Restaurant servers claim card transactions failed and request multiple retry attempts. All attempts actually process successfully, resulting in triple-charging. A November 2024 incident at Niwa Cafe Miyama saw three charges approved despite claims of failure, with the restaurant unresponsive to refund requests. How to avoid: Request to see every receipt (declined and approved) before leaving. Check your banking app in real time before retrying failed transactions. Pay cash where possible on Miyajima. Photograph terminal screens as evidence. Dispute with your bank immediately via chargeback rather than relying on merchant refunds.

Scam alert in Hiroshima, Japan — The Miyajima Omotesando Souvenir Markup (sightseeing, severity: low). You step off the Miyajima ferry and walk into the first shop on Omotesando — the 300-meter shopping street between the pier and Itsukushima Shrine. A box of ten momiji manju (maple-leaf-shaped cakes) is ¥1,400. The exact same box at Nishiki-do in Hiroshima Station is ¥1,050 — a 33% premium for walking through the door. Further along the street, shops label factory-wrapped manju 'handmade Miyajima specialty' with no visible on-site production. The contents of the boxes are identical. How to avoid: Buy your momiji manju at Hiroshima Station before you board the ferry — Nishiki-do and Fujii-ya both have booths at the shinkansen exit, and both stock the same brands the island sells. If you want to buy on the island anyway, walk past the first 200 meters of Omotesando (where premiums concentrate) before spending anything over ¥1,000, and only buy from shops where you can see a cook actually making manju in the window — Momiji-do and Iwamura have real on-site production.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — The Gion / Pontocho Bar Hustler Hostess Trap (nightlife, severity: high). A well-dressed man approaches tourists on nightlife streets, offering recommendations to a bar with 'first drink free.' Victims are led upstairs where hostesses sit uninvited, drinks appear without ordering, and bouncers block exits. Final bills reach ¥60,000+ for watered whisky and undisclosed company fees. Kyoto's anti-kyakuhiki ordinance (since 2015) makes street soliciting illegal citywide. How to avoid: Never follow strangers into bars you didn't independently research on Google Maps or Tabelog. Anyone approaching you on Pontocho or Gion streets is breaking local law—walk past without engagement. Always request a price list before sitting ('料金表を見せてください'). If pressured, call 110 and say 'bottakuri.' Stick to street-level izakayas with clear signage, Japanese customers, and 4.2+ ratings.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — The Gion Private-Road ¥10,000 Fine (Geisha Photo Shakedown) (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Tourists photograph people in maiko dress on Gion side streets and either encounter a 'manager' demanding ¥1,000-5,000 or face a real ¥10,000 fine enforced since April 2024 by the Gion Machi Nan-gawa Council. The council closed narrow private alleys off Hanamikoji after repeated incidents of tourists grabbing kimono sleeves and blocking maiko appointments. Signs in four languages warn of penalties; touching a maiko is criminal assault carrying up to ¥500,000 in fines and six months in jail. How to avoid: Photograph geiko and maiko only from Hanamikoji's main public road, never from side alleys with '私道・立入禁止・罰金1万円' signs. If someone demands cash for a photo, politely decline and walk toward Shijo-dori—no legal basis exists for the shakedown. Never touch, grab, or block anyone in kimono. Consider lawful geisha encounters at Gion Corner or ozashiki dinners (¥3,500-50,000) instead.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — The Arashiyama 'Dream Cafe' Bait-and-Switch (sightseeing, severity: moderate). An older woman sweeping the pavement recruits tourists into a charming-looking café promising 'Kyoto cultural experience' for ¥3,000. Inside, guests receive odd-tasting hojicha, then staff offer 'exclusive meetings with Mr Hayakawa' for ¥63,000 per hour. Dream Cafe accumulated 1.4-star reviews before Kyoto Prefectural Police raided it on fraud charges. The hustling pattern persists despite venue closure. How to avoid: Never enter Arashiyama cafés or tea-ceremony venues recruited via street hustling—hustling itself is illegal under Kyoto City ordinance. Pre-select matcha and kaiseki venues on Google Maps (4.3+ ratings, 200+ reviews) before arrival. Watch for multilingual warning signs marking known-bad blocks. Refuse bills over ¥2,000 for tea without printed pricing and call 110. Prefer established teahouses with Tabelog profiles where Japanese and English menus match exactly.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — The No-Menu Restaurant Near Kinkaku-ji / Kiyomizu (money, severity: moderate). Restaurants immediately adjacent to major sights display picture-only menus at the door with no prices. After customers commit to seating, prices are revealed, often inflating modest meals to ¥6,000+ per head (expected ¥1,500). Most-reported pattern on traveler forums after bar hustlers. Venues may charge 10% service tax plus 10% consumption tax stacked together. How to avoid: Always ask '料金は？' (how much?) before sitting. Walk two to three streets away from sights before choosing restaurants—value drops significantly. Check Tabelog (not Google Maps, which lists tourist-trap venues) before entering. If given only English menus, request Japanese versions; refusal signals foreigner-premium pricing. Avoid venues charging both '消費税10%' and 'サービス料10%' simultaneously.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — The Kyoto Airbnb / Minpaku 'Pay on Arrival' Scam (money, severity: moderate). Hosts message guests after confirmation (via WhatsApp or LINE, not the platform) demanding passport scans and extra cleaning fees not listed. Alternative patterns include properties at non-existent addresses or hosts demanding cash on arrival with promised Airbnb refunds later. Off-platform payment requests violate platform policy. Unlicensed operators seek cash to avoid paper trails. How to avoid: All payment and messaging must occur through booking platforms; report off-platform requests immediately to Airbnb/Booking.com. Passport checks are legally required but performed face-to-face on arrival only—never upload scans to host-provided URLs. Verify properties display minpaku license numbers (6-digit codes like M230000000) at entry and in listings. If hosts cancel last-minute, let the platform rebook you at their cost. Prefer central Kyoto hotels (Shijo, Karasuma, Kawaramachi) for first-time visitors.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — The Unlicensed 'White Taxi' (Shirotaku) from Kansai Airport and Kyoto Station (transport, severity: moderate). Plainclothes drivers approach exhausted arrivals at Kansai Airport or Kyoto Station offering flat-rate 'taxi' rides (¥15,000 KIX-Kyoto or ¥5,000-8,000 locally). Vehicles display white license plates instead of green taxi plates. Drivers are uninsured, unlicensed, unregulated on fares, and linked to organized crime; October 2024 and January 2026 arrests involved 10 Chinese nationals operating these rings. How to avoid: Use only official taxi queues at Kansai Airport and Kyoto Station (Hachijo and Karasuma exits); look for green license plates, company logos, and 空車 (available) lights. Take JR Haruka Express (¥2,900-3,600), Keihan Bus, or prebooked MK Skygate Shuttle (¥4,400) from Kansai. For Kyoto Station to Gion: metered official taxi (¥1,500-2,000) or Subway Karasuma Line (¥220). Use Japan Taxi / Go / Uber apps for licensed dispatches with photo/receipt documentation.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — The Fake Buddhist Monk Bracelet Donation (other, severity: low). Men in saffron or black robes place unsolicited gold-foil bracelets or cards into tourists' hands, bow deeply, then open donation registers showing names with ¥5,000-10,000 entries—implying expected matching contributions. The 'blessing' is theater; real Japanese Buddhist monks do not solicit from strangers on streets. Pattern documented at Fushimi Inari, Kinkaku-ji, Gion, and near temples. How to avoid: Keep walking and refuse anything handed to you—'No thank you' with a head shake is culturally acceptable. Donate to Kyoto temples only through fixed collection boxes (saisen-bako) inside main halls. If an item is placed in your hand, calmly return it and continue walking; no obligation exists. Real Kyoto monks wear sect-specific dark robes and travel in groups or to known locations; lone 'monks' in bright saffron on Gion streets are scammers. Alert temple staff at nearest shrine office.

Scam alert in Kyoto, Japan — Hidden Cover Charge / Otoshi Shock at Gion & Pontocho Izakayas (money, severity: low). A small dish of pickled vegetables appears before ordering—this is otoshi (お通し), a legitimate ¥300-800 per-person seating fee standard in Japanese izakaya culture. However, predatory tourist-zone venues inflate it to ¥2,000-3,000 per person, often combined with ¥500 oshibori fees, ¥1,000 seat charges, and 10% service taxes stacked with 10% consumption tax, tripling bills. How to avoid: Before sitting ask '席料とお通しはいくらですか？' (how much are seat charge and otoshi?). Understand otoshi is normal—¥300-800 per person is standard; ¥1,000+ is predatory. Refusing politely is possible ('お通しは結構です') but some venues refuse seating. Check Tabelog where otoshi prices appear in reviews. Demand itemized receipts (領収書) before paying—a legal right. Look for Tabelog 3.5+ ratings explicitly noting 'no table charge' or chains like Torikizoku with all-inclusive pricing.

Scam alert in Nara, Japan — The Nara Park Deer Antler & Bite Injury (sightseeing, severity: high). Visitors purchase shika senbei crackers near Todai-ji and become surrounded by wild deer that bite, nip, and occasionally inflict antler wounds. The Nara Prefectural Government documented 159 injury cases in fiscal 2024, with 111 involving tourists. September–October mating season sees heightened aggression, with September 2024 alone producing 35 injuries and 10 hospitalizations—a sevenfold increase year-over-year. How to avoid: Purchase and distribute one pack of crackers quickly rather than teasing. Keep hands raised and empty when out of food. Avoid stags with full antlers August–November. Never allow children to feed deer unattended. Read multilingual warning pamphlets. Wash any bite wounds with tap water and contact the Nara Deer Preservation Foundation at +81-742-22-2388 for serious injuries.

Scam alert in Nara, Japan — The Sanjo-dori / Higashimuki-dori Souvenir Shakedown (other, severity: low). Generic souvenir shops along the approach to Todai-ji charge 2–3 times department-store prices for keychains, fans, and cakes. More significantly, shopkeepers exhibit rude behavior toward foreign tourists, including shouting and spraying water at visitors lingering outside storefronts. Multiple Google Maps reviews document dismissive treatment and forced exits. How to avoid: Skip Sanjo-dori and Higashimuki-dori strips; purchase identical items at Don Quijote or Kintetsu Nara department store for 30–50% savings. Visit branded craft specialists instead of generic souvenir shops. Avoid bus-tour captive venues. Check Google Maps ratings—anything under 3.8★ is a reliable warning sign. Report aggressive behavior to Nara's Tourist Information Center at Kintetsu Nara Station 2F.

Scam alert in Nara, Japan — The Nara Ryokan Bait-and-Switch (money, severity: moderate). Guests book traditional ryokan accommodations based on appealing photos but experience room downgrades upon arrival with vague justifications. Properties like Wakasa Bettei and Hotel New Wakasa have clustered complaints describing "おとり広告" (bait-and-switch advertising). Issues include switched rooms, non-functional outdoor baths, double-billing disputes, and refusal to process cancellations or refunds. How to avoid: Book only properties with 50+ English reviews and 4.2+ ratings, weighing recent reviews heavily. Screenshot exact room and amenity photos before booking. Photograph check-in bills. Obtain written email confirmation of all cancellations—automated replies alone are insufficient. Avoid double-booking across platforms. Prefer Japan Ryokan Association-certified properties or established chains. Report fraud immediately to Booking.com, Rakuten Travel, or Jalan.

Scam alert in Nara, Japan — The Nara Taxi Long-Route Detour (transport, severity: low). Taxi drivers take unnecessarily long routes to inflate fares, such as routing a 2 km trip via prefectural roads to create a 6.8 km detour. Drivers may ask passengers to confirm route names rather than entering destinations into GPS. Nara Kintetsu Taxi (2.5★ / 62 reviews) and sister company Kai-Nara Taxi (1.9–2.0★) both display clustered complaints about meter-running and rude behavior. How to avoid: Use the GO taxi app for Nara Kintetsu Taxi—it displays routes and fares before boarding. Show drivers Google Maps with highlighted routes and decline verbal alternatives. Walk distances under 2 km (Kintetsu Nara Station to Todai-ji is ~20 minutes). Use the Nara City Loop Bus or rail for station transfers. Prefer higher-rated stands: 近鉄奈良駅前観光タクシー乗り場 (4.0★) or 近鉄奈良駅前中型タクシー乗り場 (5.0★). Only use green-plate licensed taxis.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Matsuyama Kyabakura / Bottakuri Bar Overcharge (nightlife, severity: high). You're walking through Matsuyama in Naha after dinner and a hustler in a suit pitches 'great bar upstairs, ¥3,000 set.' You take the elevator to the fourth floor, the room is dim, and the door clicks shut behind you. A bottle of 'champagne' arrives unrequested. Ninety minutes later the bill is ¥821,000 — the exact amount in a March 2021 documented case for seven bottles of champagne and six juices. July 2023 police raids on Matsuyama found 18 establishments paying yakuza protection money, and the entire district sits on the Okinawa Prefectural Police caution list. How to avoid: Never take an elevator to an upstairs bar you were pulled into from the street in Matsuyama. Stay on Kokusai-dori — it is well-lit, ground-floor, and tourist-safe. If you're already inside and staff ask for your card before showing a printed menu with prices, stand up and leave; no order placed means no legal claim. If the door is blocked, dial 110 — Okinawa Prefectural Police run a dedicated bottakuri response unit for Matsuyama. Freeze the card from your issuer's app at the first sign of coercion.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Makishi Public Market Cooking-Fee Bait-and-Switch (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Fish vendors at Makishi Public Market quote unpriced seafood then charge ¥550-per-person cooking fees upstairs, including for non-eating family members. February 2026 review documented charging for 5 people when only 2 were eating. Prices change based on customer nationality with no posted rates. How to avoid: Get fish prices in writing before purchase leaves counter. Confirm cooking-fee headcount in advance. Walk away from stalls refusing written pricing. Use Tomari Fish Market instead where prices are posted. Demand itemized receipt.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Naha Airport Shirotaku and Long-Distance Taxi Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Illegal white-plate taxis (shirotaku) at airport arrivals refuse meters and charge 1.5× normal fares with no receipt. Even licensed Stand No.8 is rated 2.3 stars with drivers inflating fares via unnecessary expressway detours and forcing large taxis instead of medium vehicles. How to avoid: Use Yui Rail monorail instead (¥270-330). Queue at Stand No.6 or No.7, not Stand No.8. Insist drivers use meters before departure. Book hotel transfers or use Go taxi app. Never follow unofficial curbside ride offers.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Rental Car "Neighbor Gas Station" Fuel Overcharge (transport, severity: moderate). Rental car return counters direct customers to adjacent gas stations charging ¥197/L when market price is ¥165/L, creating ¥15-20/L premiums with no opportunity to comparison shop. Staff map specifically routes returns to overpriced partner stations. How to avoid: Fill up at ENEOS or Cosmo stations 2+ km away. Check prices via GoGo.gs before returning. Photograph fuel gauge at pickup and return. Photograph all car panels at pickup for damage disputes. Decline optional insurance upsells.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Kokusai-dori Souvenir Fake-Discount and Hidden Table Charge (sightseeing, severity: low). A souvenir shop on Kokusai-dori displays a Shisa lion-dog figurine with '¥4,980' crossed out in red marker and '¥1,980 — today only' written above it. The ¥4,980 was never the real price; the same figurine is ¥1,680 at Ryubo Department Store four blocks away and ¥1,280 at Naha Airport. Down the street, a restaurant with English photos in the window seats you, brings an unrequested plate of tofu and vegetables, and later charges ¥550 per person for 'otoshi' that wasn't on the outside menu. A ¥2,000 lunch ends at ¥4,500 for two people. How to avoid: Before buying any souvenir on Kokusai-dori over ¥1,000, check the same item on Amazon Japan or at Ryubo — if the Kokusai-dori price is more than 30% above Ryubo's, walk away. Naha Airport is usually cheaper still. For restaurants, ask 'otoshi wa arimasu ka?' (お通しはありますか？ — 'is there an otoshi charge?') before you sit down, and if the answer is yes, ask the price. Eating one block off Kokusai-dori, in the covered Heiwa-dori arcade or on Ukishima-dori, typically runs 30–40% less for the same dish.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The US Military Card-Fraud and Juicy-Bar Targeting (nightlife, severity: moderate). November 2024 Stars & Stripes reported 23 credit/debit card fraud cases at Kadena Air Base with charges appearing within 24 hours of Exchange/commissary purchases. Chatan and Kin-town juicy bars target service members with champagne pushes and drink-spiking, with specific establishments on III MEF off-limits lists. How to avoid: Check MCIPAC-MCBB Bulletin 5800 off-limits list before visiting entertainment districts. Use credit over debit off-base. Set transaction alerts on all military banking. Pay cash at small bars. Leave immediately if drink tastes wrong and contact base clinic or call 110.

Scam alert in Okinawa, Japan — The Yonaguni and Rural Okinawa Ore-Ore Police-Impersonation Fraud (money, severity: moderate). Fake police officers call hotel rooms claiming accounts are used for fraud, directing transfers to fake safe accounts. A September 2024 tourist from Niigata lost ¥19 million; a Yonaguni visitor lost over ¥10 million. January-February 2026 saw 85 fraud cases with ¥400 million in losses. How to avoid: Hang up immediately on cold police calls—Japanese police never call about accounts. Dial 110 independently to verify. Never transfer money to phone-identified accounts. Alert hotel staff of alarming calls. Never accept offers to visit ATMs from taxi drivers or strangers.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Kuromon Market Tourist-Tier Pricing (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Vendors at Kuromon Market systematically overcharge foreign tourists for seafood and wagyu. Prices are hidden, displayed only in foreign currencies, or obscured behind secondary signs. A 2024 investigation documented ¥30,000 for four crab legs and ¥3,500 for a single shrimp, though prices moderated after market association intervention. About 25 of 150 stalls carry the overcharging reputation. How to avoid: Ask exact total price in Japanese before ordering and walk away if staff dodge the question. Eat at Tenjinbashisuji Shopping Street or standalone sushi restaurants on Tabelog instead. Photograph price signs before ordering. Verify the shop displays the association's fair-price flyer.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Dotonbori Wagyu Hamburger Bait-and-Switch (nightlife, severity: high). Street hustlers lure tourists into unmarked restaurants with laminated menus advertising A5 wagyu. Once seated, staff claim card-only payment via portable readers with no cash register. Cold, poor-quality meat arrives and the bill—around ¥29,568—is already processed. October 2025 Reddit post documenting this drew 800+ upvotes confirming the pattern. How to avoid: Never follow street hustlers in Dotonbori. Pre-select wagyu restaurants on Tabelog with 4.0+ stars and 100+ Japanese reviews. Legitimate places have visible cash registers and published prices. If trapped, stand and leave before ordering; staff cannot legally force payment without an order.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Minami/Kitashinchi Girls-Bar Bottakuri (nightlife, severity: high). Hustlers offer girls bars at ¥3,000 per hour. Bills escalate to ¥300,000–¥950,000 after staff pressure customers to order expensive champagne bottles (¥200,000+). Door staff block exits; ATM withdrawal is 'suggested.' A January 2025 Suita case involved ¥950,000 charges and a January 2019 case resulted in police arrest after customers were beaten over payment disputes. How to avoid: Never enter bars recruited from the street. Book Tabelog-listed venues with published prices and 20+ Japanese reviews. Leave before accepting food or drink if no menu appears. Say '警察を呼んでください' (call police) and dial 110 if challenged. Never let staff accompany you to ATMs.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Midosuji Line Panhandle Scam (money, severity: low). You're on the Midosuji Line between Namba and Umeda and a well-dressed young man sits next to you. 'Sorry, can I practice my English?' Two minutes later the story lands: his wallet was stolen at Kansai Airport, his hotel won't let him in without ID, the police 'can't help foreigners,' and he just needs ¥5,000 to ¥10,000 for cab fare home. A July 2025 Reddit thread documented the exact script, and a nearby Japanese commuter in the same thread confirmed the operator had been working the Midosuji Line for months — tourists see the sequence once, but he runs it many times a day. How to avoid: Genuine Japanese homeless almost never approach strangers, and genuinely stranded tourists go to the koban outside every major Osaka Metro station (there's one at the south exit of Namba Station and one at the north exit of Umeda Station). If a stranger on the train opens with 'can I practice my English?' and the conversation turns to money in under three minutes, stand up at the next stop, walk off, and don't explain yourself. If they follow you off the train, walk straight into the station koban — which will end the approach instantly.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Kansai/Itami Airport Unofficial Taxi (transport, severity: moderate). Suited men approach in arrivals offering 'flat-rate' taxi service bypassing official queues. White license plates indicate unauthorized shiro-taku drivers. Initial quotes (¥8,000) inflate to ¥15,000–¥32,000 with surprise tolls and night-service fees. A 2024 case charged ¥11,640 on a ¥3,000 route; another saw ¥32,000 versus the legal ¥20,000–¥22,000 fixed rate. How to avoid: Walk directly to official taxi ranks—ignore anyone approaching in arrivals. Take Nankai Rapi:t (¥1,450) or JR Kansai-Airport Rapid (¥1,210) instead. Check that license plates are green (緑ナンバー)—white plates mean the driver is unlicensed. Photograph receipt, plate, and driver ID if charged unexpectedly and file a Kansai Transport Bureau complaint.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Counterfeit Brand Goods in Shinsaibashi/Amemura (counterfeit, severity: moderate). Luxury items (Louis Vuitton wallets at ¥8,000, Moncler jackets at ¥15,000) sold from back-street shops are counterfeit. A 2024 Mainichi investigation documented the Tsuruhashi area nicknamed '鶴橋偽ブランド通り' where sellers ask 'You're not the police, right?' before revealing stock. Osaka Customs blocked ~9,600 counterfeits in FY2024; Japanese counterfeiting carries 10-year prison and ~$73,000 USD fines. How to avoid: Prices 10–20% below retail are counterfeit. Buy only from official boutiques or major department stores (Hankyu, Daimaru, Takashimaya). Use secondhand authenticators with 50+ Japanese reviews (Komehyo, RagTag). Avoid Expo 2025 Myaku-Myaku merchandise from unofficial stalls. Do not export counterfeits—customs in EU, UK, US, Australia, South Korea will seize goods and levy fines.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Osaka Expo 2025 Fake-Ticket Fraud (money, severity: moderate). Osaka Expo 2025 ran from April to October 2025 and drew over 28 million visitors. During the run, fake websites mimicked the official Expo site, harvested card details, and sold counterfeit tickets whose QR codes failed at the gates; a March 2025 Trend Micro report flagged multiple fraudulent domains, and NHK and the Expo Association issued repeated warnings through the summer. Since the Expo closed, the same operators have pivoted to selling counterfeit Myaku-Myaku mascot merchandise through look-alike shops. A typical victim is charged around ¥7,500 to ¥15,000 for a 'limited-edition' plush that either never arrives or arrives as a poor knockoff from a foreign warehouse. How to avoid: Expo 2025 closed in October 2025—any site selling 'Expo tickets' in 2026 is a scam. Buy Myaku-Myaku merchandise only from official licensees (Osaka Tourism Bureau shops and major department stores such as Hankyu, Daimaru, or Takashimaya). Never click Expo-themed ads on social media. If you've already paid a suspicious site, file a chargeback with your card issuer within 60 days and report the site to the Consumer Affairs Agency hotline on 188.

Scam alert in Osaka, Japan — Dotonbori Pickpocketing and Phone-Hold Distraction (other, severity: high). Thieves target dense crowds at Dotonbori's Ebisu Bridge Glico sign photo spot (500+ tourists) and Namba Walk. Phones in back pockets vanish; a classic distraction involves asking you to hold someone's phone while taking a photo—while distracted, an accomplice rifles your bag. A 2025 NTV report featured a 41-year-old serial thief rearrested after CCTV caught him stealing a ¥35,000 wallet from a backpack; he told police 'Japanese people are easy targets.' How to avoid: Wear a cross-body bag with zipper forward or money belt under clothes. Never put valuables in back or open jacket pockets. At Glico Bridge, stand with back to wall, not in crowd center. Don't hand your phone to strangers—ask uniformed staff instead. On Midosuji Line during rush hour, wear backpack on front. Report theft to nearest koban immediately for insurance purposes.

Scam alert in Sapporo, Japan — The Susukino Hustler Bar Rip-Off (Bottakuri) (nightlife, severity: high). Street hustlers in Susukino approach visitors claiming to warn about rip-off bars, then lead them to overpriced venues where hidden charges, inflated drink prices, and mandatory fees accumulate rapidly. A documented case involved a ¥343,200 tab including champagne priced over ¥200,000 per bottle. Victims report being blocked from leaving until payment is made or cards are surrendered. How to avoid: Never follow street hustlers or use free information booths in Susukino, as both are illegal under the 2022 ordinance. Pick bars in advance via Tabelog or Google Maps. Ask about seating charges and request full menus before sitting. Pay cash only, keep cards and passport secure, photograph menus, and call 110 if trapped.

Scam alert in Sapporo, Japan — The Host Club Tsukebarai (Tab-Debt) Trap for Women (nightlife, severity: high). Host clubs and men's concept cafes target female customers with romantic manipulation, encouraging high-spending tsukebarai (tab/credit) debts. Once debt accumulates beyond ability to pay, clubs refer customers to illegal sex-work brokers. A 2024 investigation documented seven arrests involving a ring earning over ¥100 million annually through this scheme. How to avoid: Never accept tsukebarai tabs; leave immediately if unable to pay in cash. Treat romantic overtures as sales scripts. Set nightly cash limits, leave cards at hotels, and refuse champagne tower invitations. If offered 'easier work' or referred to sex shops, contact Hokkaido Police sex-crime line at 0120-028-110.

Scam alert in Sapporo, Japan — The Nijo Market "Inbound-Don" Overcharge (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Nijo Market restaurants charge tourists ¥3,000-¥4,000 for mediocre kaisendon bowls that cost ¥1,500-¥2,500 elsewhere, and ¥500 per mantis shrimp when Daimaru sells two for ¥600. English and Chinese menus signal inflated pricing; local-language prices are absent or minimized. How to avoid: Visit Jogai (Central Wholesale Outer) Market near Sapporo Station instead, where prices are roughly half. If eating at Nijo, use only Japanese-language menus and confirm total price beforehand. Buy crab at New Chitose Airport duty-free, bring cash, and budget no more than ¥2,500 for kaisendon.

Scam alert in Sapporo, Japan — The Susukino Crab-Buffet "All You Can Eat" Trap (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Tourist-chain crab restaurants advertise ¥6,000-¥10,000 all-you-can-eat buffets where the first serving is fresh but subsequent plates are lower-grade or near-spoiled. Staff dig through trash to enforce finish-the-plate policies, use strict timers to force drink orders, and serve frozen product despite 'live' claims. How to avoid: Skip tour-bus chains like Nanda, Ebi-Kani-Gassen, and Kani Shogun. Book small à-la-carte crab specialists where quality can be judged per dish. Read recent Google 1-star reviews before booking. Buy vacuum-sealed crab at New Chitose Airport instead. Bring cash and confirm total pricing beforehand.

Scam alert in Sapporo, Japan — The Ramen Yokocho Tourist-Alley Bait-and-Switch (sightseeing, severity: low). Ganso Sapporo Ramen Yokocho's 17 shops charge ¥1,200-¥1,500 for miso ramen versus ¥900-¥1,100 nearby. Service to foreigners is dismissive, toppings are frozen, and shops close unpredictably or refuse walk-ins despite empty seats. One review documented a blue glove fragment in broth. How to avoid: Skip the famous alley; visit Sumire, Ramen Shingen, Menya Saimi, or ramen shops at New Chitose Airport instead. If visiting Yokocho, check individual shop Google reviews from the last six months. Avoid shops with aggressive hosts outside. Visit before 11:30 AM or after 2 PM to avoid tour buses.

Scam alert in Sapporo, Japan — The "Free Information Booth" (無料案内所) Kickback Scheme (nightlife, severity: moderate). Neon-signed 'Free Information' kiosks throughout Susukino are commission-paid referral agencies, not tourist information offices. They direct clients to partner bars paying the highest commissions regardless of customer requests. Final bills do not match brochure prices, and the booth becomes unreachable when complaints arise. How to avoid: Never use 無料案内所 booths; use Google Maps, Tabelog, or HOT PEPPER Gourmet instead. Book venues directly via their websites or phone numbers. Walk alone to chosen venues and refuse escorts from booth staff. Call consumer hotline 188 for misrepresentation complaints.

Scam alert in Sapporo, Japan — The Sapporo Hotel-Parking Non-Refund Trap (transport, severity: low). You reserved a hotel in central Sapporo and pre-paid ¥3,000 for two nights of on-site parking. You arrive in a rented Toyota Alphard from New Chitose Airport. The valet tries three times and the mechanical stacker rejects the vehicle — too tall, too heavy, or too long (most hotel stackers cap at 1.55 m height, 1,900 kg weight, 5.05 m length). The front desk apologizes and refuses to refund the parking fee. You now pay ¥1,500 to ¥2,000 per night at the nearest coin lot and eat the ¥3,000 you already spent. How to avoid: Before booking, email the hotel directly — not through the OTA — with the rental car's exact length, width, height, and weight (Toyota and Nissan rental pages list them) and ask for written confirmation that the stacker accepts it. Rental SUVs and minivans almost never fit. Either downsize to a compact (Yaris, Note, Fit), stay at a hotel near Sapporo Station with a surface lot (JR Tower Hotel Nikko and Mitsui Garden Hotel both have one), or skip the car entirely — the Rapid Airport train is ¥1,150 and 37 minutes from New Chitose to Sapporo Station.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Kabukicho Bottakuri Bar Overcharge (nightlife, severity: high). A street hustler offers 'first drink free' or 'cheap beer' and leads you into a basement or upper-floor bar. After two or three drinks, the bill reaches ¥130,000 to ¥510,000 with staff blocking the door. Shinjuku Police logged approximately 190 complaints totaling roughly ¥140 million in the first ten months of 2024 alone. How to avoid: Never follow a street hustler in Kabukicho, Roppongi, Shibuya, or Ikebukuro. Pick bars yourself from Google Maps with 4.5+ stars and 100+ English reviews. Demand a printed menu with yen prices before ordering. Carry only cash you plan to spend. If overcharged, call 110 and say 'bottakuri' or dispute via credit card the same day. Do not sign any slip or receipt.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Kabukicho Drink-Spike + Face ID Crypto Drain (nightlife, severity: high). A friendly hustler named 'Ron' or 'Ken' invites you to a bar where your second drink is stronger than expected. You wake at 6 a.m. with an empty wallet—and if crypto was on your phone, your Coinbase or MetaMask wallet has been drained via Face ID. One documented case involved a $20,000 cryptocurrency loss. How to avoid: Turn off Face ID and Touch ID on your phone before going out at night; require a 6+ digit PIN instead. Never leave your drink unattended. Keep crypto on a hardware wallet in your hotel safe. If suddenly intoxicated, walk to the Kabukicho koban or flag a police officer. Do not settle the bill—leave immediately. If drugged, go to a hospital for a medical record before contacting police.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Violent Shinjuku Hustler Ambush (nightlife, severity: high). A man in a puffer jacket blocks your path with photos of girls on a smartphone. When you try to walk around, he sidesteps to stay in front of you. This has escalated to physical attacks, with hustlers locking exits and robbing customers. Tokyo Metropolitan Police made 390+ kyakuhiki arrests in 2024. How to avoid: Do not stop walking or make eye contact with hustlers. Walk on well-lit main drags rather than side streets after midnight. If blocked, loudly say '警察を呼ぶ' (keisatsu o yobu—I'll call the police) and walk past. If physically grabbed, shout to draw attention. Travel in groups of two or more after dark. Use Shinjuku City's anti-kyakuhiki reporting line.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Matching-App Bar Lure (nightlife, severity: high). You match on Tinder, Bumble, Pairs, or Tapple with someone who suggests 'a nice bar I know' in Kabukicho or Nishi-Azabu. After one or two drinks, the bill is ¥70,000 to ¥1,100,000. The person was paid per delivered customer. In May 2025, police reported a ring that netted ¥80 million from 50+ male victims. How to avoid: Insist on a venue YOU pick from Google Maps with 4.5+ stars and 100+ English reviews. If the match refuses your suggestion more than once, unmatch immediately. Meet for coffee or a walk in daylight first. Never let a matching-app meetup lead to an unvetted bar. If inside and the menu has no prices, stand up and leave before ordering. Call Tokyo Metropolitan Police Shinjuku Division and say 'マッチングアプリ ぼったくり'.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Yurakucho / Ginza 'HAMANOKA'-style Yakitori Overcharge (nightlife, severity: moderate). A staff member waves you into a yakitori spot under the JR tracks. No English menu appears until after you're seated. What seemed reasonable becomes a bill 2–3x higher with otoshi charges, seat charges, and drinks you don't remember ordering. Victims report paying over ¥10,000 for two people for three non-alcoholic drinks and small plates. How to avoid: Pick your yakitori from Google Maps or Tabelog with 4.0+ stars and recent Japanese reviews before leaving your hotel. Ask 'Seat料はいくらですか?' before ordering. Demand an itemized receipt—this is your legal right. Avoid places claiming Torikizoku affiliation; 15 people were arrested in January 2024 for this impersonation. Dispute with your credit card company the same day if overcharged.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Narita / Haneda Unlicensed 'Shirotaku' Taxi (transport, severity: moderate). Before reaching the official taxi queue at Haneda or Narita, a man in a suit offers a 'fixed price' ride to Shinjuku in a white-plated car. There is no commercial insurance, no meter, and the quoted price often increases on arrival. A legitimate flat-rate taxi from Haneda to Shinjuku is ¥8,300; unlicensed taxis charge significantly more. Police reported 113 shirotaku arrests in Jan–Oct 2025—a 10x increase over 2021. How to avoid: Use only the official airport taxi queue. Green license plates indicate legal taxis; white plates indicate illegal shirotaku. Official Haneda to Shinjuku flat rate is ¥8,300 (zone A) as of 2025; Narita to Shinjuku is approximately ¥22,500. Use Uber Japan or the Go app for transparent pricing. Better yet, take the Keikyu or Tokyo Monorail from Haneda (¥600) or Narita Express (¥3,270). Never share your hotel address with someone who approached you first.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Fake Monk / Bracelet Donation Scam (sightseeing, severity: low). A person in saffron robes (sometimes grey) presses a small gold plastic bracelet or prayer card into your hand near Sensoji's Thunder Gate or other major temples. A donation book then appears—the 'gift' suddenly costs ¥3,000 to ¥10,000. Ueno Toshogu Shrine issued a July 2023 public warning specifically calling this out, noting the scammer has no shrine affiliation. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets or hold your bag strap when passing someone in religious robes near tourist sites. Do not accept anything placed in your hand—drop it back immediately. Walk briskly away if they insist; they rarely follow more than 20 meters. Real donations are made inside temples at saisen-bako (offering boxes), never on the street. Use the official merchandise counter (授与所) inside temples if you wish to genuinely support them.

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Tokyo Taxi Nighttime Detour (transport, severity: moderate). You hail a taxi at 2 a.m. outside a Roppongi club for a ¥1,200 ride to your hotel, but it becomes ¥4,500 with an unexplained detour. The driver gestures 'construction' or 'one way' when questioned. While Tokyo taxis are generally honest, detours concentrate between 22:00 and 05:00 when the legal 20% late-night surcharge applies and scrutiny is reduced. How to avoid: Use the Go or S.RIDE app for pre-set fares and tracked drivers. Show your destination to the driver in Japanese address format via Google Maps before you get in. Follow the route on your phone in real time and speak up if it diverges. Ask for the ryoshusho (receipt)—they must provide one with the company's dispute line. Plan to be home before the last train (around 00:30) or stay out until the first train (around 05:00).

Scam alert in Tokyo, Japan — The Tourist-Area Photographer / Guide Deposit Ghost (other, severity: moderate). You book a 'freelance Tokyo photographer' on Instagram for a kimono shoot at Sensoji. You pay a ¥15,000–¥40,000 deposit. They show up, take photos, and then ghost—no edited images, no replies, and the Instagram account disappears within a week. Photography services are not covered by standard travel platform refund policies. How to avoid: Book only through platforms with built-in refund protection: Airbnb Experiences, Klook, Viator, or GetYourGuide—avoid direct Instagram DMs. Pay by credit card (not debit, cash, or transfer) for chargeback protection. Verify the photographer's Instagram is at least one year old with consistent posting. Reverse-image-search portfolio shots to check for stolen images. Video-call the photographer before paying. Keep deposits small (¥5,000 or less) with balance due on delivery of edited files.

Scam alert in Yokohama, Japan — The Fukutomicho Drug-and-Charge Blackout Scam (nightlife, severity: high). Hustlers near Kannai or Isezakicho approach tourists offering cheap girls bars. Victims follow them into snack bars in Fukutomicho where they consume drinks potentially spiked with substances, lose consciousness, and wake with unauthorized charges exceeding ¥600,000. Police documented 249 victims losing ¥147.39 million in 11 months of 2023, with one victim charged ¥2.7 million in a single night. How to avoid: Treat Fukutomicho as a no-go zone after dark. Never follow hustlers (now illegal under May 2025 ordinance). Refuse drinks you didn't watch poured. Stay on main Noge streets with open-front venues. Set low ATM withdrawal limits and card transaction caps before traveling. Contact Isezaki Police Station if blackout and unauthorized charges occur.

Scam alert in Yokohama, Japan — The Chinatown All-You-Can-Eat 6-Order Limit & Leftover Surcharge (sightseeing, severity: moderate). Chinatown all-you-can-eat restaurants advertise unlimited dining at ¥2,500 for 90 minutes but enforce hidden rules: only 6 items ordered at once, with leftovers triggering surcharges up to ¥15,000 never displayed on street signage or menus. Rules are announced only after customers sit down. How to avoid: Only eat at shops with Yokohama Chinatown Development Association certification plaques. Stick to venues rated 4.3+ with 500+ Japanese reviews. Avoid plainclothes hustlers soliciting outside. Ask explicitly about order limits and leftover surcharges in writing before sitting. Photograph menus and posted rules. Prefer family-style or shops advertising 食べ残し無料 (no leftover surcharge).

Scam alert in Yokohama, Japan — The Yokohama Station West Exit Hustler-Izakaya Trap (nightlife, severity: moderate). Hustlers with clipboards near Yokohama Station West Exit approach tourists with offers of ¥1,300 all-you-can-drink specials. After collecting ¥500-1,000 upfront 'deposits,' venues add undisclosed mandatory minimums, service charges, and premium otoshi fees that double the advertised price. How to avoid: Pre-book venues on Tabelog or Google Maps before leaving your hotel. Exit via East Exit or Minatomirai walkway to avoid hustler concentration. Never hand cash deposits to hustlers. Ask explicitly about otoshi, service charges, and minimum-order rules before sitting. Call 110 and cite the Kanagawa Nuisance Prevention Ordinance if pressured.

Scam alert in Yokohama, Japan — The Noge Girls Bar / Komachi-dori Hostess Overcharge (nightlife, severity: high). You're having a good night in Noge and a friendly man on Komachi-dori says, 'Hey, nice girls bar, ¥3,000 per hour, drinks included.' You follow him up a narrow stairwell to a dim room on the third floor. Two hostesses sit at your table the moment you do. Ninety minutes later the bill is ¥112,000: the hostesses' time at ¥8,000 each per 30 minutes, a ¥15,000 bottle of sparkling wine you never ordered, a ¥5,000 cover charge, and a ¥3,000 service fee. No printed menu ever appeared. Under Yokohama's May 2025 solicitation ordinance, the street approach itself is now illegal, but enforcement is still catching up. How to avoid: Never follow anyone from the street into an upstairs bar in Noge or Isezaki-cho. Stay on ground-floor venues with a printed menu visible from outside — most Noge izakaya with 4.5+ Google ratings and 500+ Japanese reviews fit that test. If you're already seated somewhere without a menu, stand up and leave before the first drink is poured; staff have no legal claim on you while no order has been placed. If you're blocked from leaving, say 'keisatsu wo yonde kudasai' (警察を呼んでください — 'please call the police') and dial 110 yourself. Under the May 2025 ordinance, officers will come.

Scam alert in Yokohama, Japan — The Chinatown Sweet Chestnut Sample-Then-Force-Sell (sightseeing, severity: low). You're walking down the main street of Yokohama Chinatown and a vendor holds out a paper cone of warm amaguri — roasted sweet chestnuts — with a smile. You take one. The moment the sample is in your mouth, the vendor is already scooping a full one-kilogram bag, weighing it on a scale, and handing it to you for ¥3,800. Refusing in front of fifty passing tourists feels impossible. That's the design. Legitimate confectioners near the South Gate sell the same item, packaged and priced in a window display, for around ¥1,200 per 500 g. How to avoid: Keep your hands in your pockets when passing amaguri stalls that offer samples, and say 'kekkou desu' (結構です — 'no thank you') before the vendor reaches out. If you've already taken a sample, smile, wave it off with 'kekkou desu,' and walk away — the vendor cannot chase you down Chinatown's main street, and you owe nothing for an unsolicited sample. Buy chestnuts from a named confectioner with per-bag prices visible from the sidewalk; Shoukoushuuka and Edoseikaro near the South Gate are safe defaults, and Yokohama Chinatown Development Association-certified stalls display a seal in the window.

Scam alert in Yokohama, Japan — The Yokohama Station / Haneda Airport Taxi Meter Games (transport, severity: low). Taxi drivers at Yokohama Station West Exit quote discounts then add mystery surcharges pushing fares ¥2,000 over standard meter rates. At Haneda Airport, independent operators repeatedly toggle highway-mode during rides, inflating ¥7,000 trips to ¥8,000+. How to avoid: Use only official licensed taxi queues with green license plates. Pre-check expected fares on NAVITIME or GO app before boarding. Request itemized receipts (領収書) by law. Use GO or Uber apps for upfront fare computation. For Haneda-to-Yokohama, take Keikyu Airport Line (¥500) or Limousine Bus (¥650) instead. Report overcharges with plate photos to Kanagawa Transport Bureau or 110.
